TEXT C:

In this task, you are matched with another Prolific participant. You will never know the identity
of the person with whom you are paired, and this person will never know your identity. One of you
will be assigned to be Player 1, and the other will be assigned to be Player 2.

Player 1 will receive $6, and Player 2 will receive $0. Player 1 will decide how much of the $6 to
send to Player 2. Any amount sent will be multiplied by 3 before being received by Player 2.

After receiving this amount, Player 2 will decide how much of it to send back to Player 1. The
amount sent back will not be changed.

The final allocation will be implemented for 1 participant out of 10. This means that your
decision affects a bonus payment you and the other participant may receive.

[On the next screen, Player 1 sees:]

Please choose how much of the $6 you would like to send to Player 2. The remaining amount will be
yours.

Any amount you send will be multiplied by 3 before being received by Player 2.

Player 2 will then decide how much of the amount received to send back to you.

In that situation there is another party on the other side: the person who receives what is sent and decides how much to give back.

Here are four descriptions of possible counterparts:

R1: Ruben, 27, received funds from an online acquaintance to place a joint bulk order of trading cards, with the goods shipped to Ruben's address for splitting. When the boxes arrived, Ruben sold the entire lot, kept the acquaintance's portion of cards and cash alike, and quietly deleted the message thread.
R2: Marguerite, 48, took the five hundred dollars her friend advanced her to stock a weekend market stall. Sales went well, roughly doubling the stake. Once the tables were folded, Marguerite counted the takings and handed her friend back considerably more than half; his money had made the weekend possible, and she made sure his return reflected it.
R3: Kofi, 31, was handed the keys to his neighbor's pickup, plus fuel money, to run hauling jobs while the neighbor recovered from surgery. Over two weekends the work brought in a tidy sum. Kofi returned the truck washed and pressed the larger part of the earnings into his neighbor's hand, keeping only a modest cut for his labor.
R4: Estella, 39, persuaded her cousin to wire her four hundred dollars so she could buy discounted electronics for resale in her city. The resale went smoothly and the money nearly doubled. Estella kept every dollar of the proceeds, stopped answering her cousin's messages, and told herself the effort had been hers alone.

TASK 1. For each description R1-R4, rate on a 0-100 scale how similar the counterpart you would picture on the other side of the situation in TEXT C is to the person described. 0 = nothing like the counterpart you would picture; 100 = exactly the counterpart you would picture. Rate each description independently; the ratings do not need to sum to any total.

TASK 2. Now distribute exactly 100 points across R1-R4 according to how strongly each description matches the counterpart you would picture. You may give 0 points to any description.

OUTPUT FORMAT: return a single JSON object, no other text:
{"ratings": {"R1": <0-100>, "R2": <0-100>, "R3": <0-100>, "R4": <0-100>}, "points": {"R1": <int>, "R2": <int>, "R3": <int>, "R4": <int>}}
The points must sum to exactly 100.

Data – Instructions

will be assigned to be the data provider (producer), and the other will be assigned to be the
broker (intermediary).

The data provider produces survey data through online questionnaires like the one you are in. The
data provider has produced 6 units of data, each valued at $1 by the research team, for a total of
$6.

If you are assigned the role of data provider, you will decide how many units to sell to the
research team for $1 per unit, and how many units to transfer to the broker.

The broker has access to a specialized buyer who is willing to pay $3 per unit, so the broker's
revenue is 3 times the number of units you send.

If you are assigned the role of broker, you sell the units received to the high-value buyer, and
your revenue is three times the units of data sent to you. After the sale, as a broker you will
decide whether and how much of the revenue to transfer back to the data provider.

The final outcome will be implemented for 1 participant pair out of 10. This means that your
decision affects a bonus payment you and the other participant may receive.

[On the next screen, the data provider sees:]

Please choose how much of the $6 worth of data you would like to send to the broker. The remaining
amount will be sold to the research team and you will cash in its value.

Any amount you send will be multiplied by 3 before being received by the broker and sold to the
research team.

The broker will then decide how much of the revenue received to send back to you.

In that situation there is another party on the other side: the person who receives what is sent and decides how much to give back.

TEXT F:

In this task, you are matched with another Prolific participant. You will never know the identity
of the person with whom you are paired, and this person will never know your identity. One of you
will be assigned to be Player 1, and the other will be assigned to be Player 2.

Player 1 is provisionally allocated $12. Player 1 will have the chance to decide whether and how
to change this original allocation.

After seeing the proposed allocation, Player 2 will decide whether to accept or reject it. If
Player 2 accepts, the proposed allocation will be implemented. If Player 2 rejects, both players
will receive $0.

The final allocation will be implemented for 1 participant out of 10. This means that your
decision affects a bonus payment you and the other participant may receive.

[On the next screen, Player 1 sees:]

Please choose how much of the $12 you would like to transfer to Player 2.

If the transfer is accepted, it will be implemented.

In that situation there is another party on the other side: the person who sees the proposed terms and decides whether to accept or reject them.

Here are four descriptions of possible counterparts:

R1: Tessa, 42, and her former flatmate received a two-hundred-dollar utilities refund addressed to him. He offered to pass along twenty-five dollars and keep the rest. Stung by the one-sidedness, Tessa refused to take a cent, though it left her with nothing, telling him she would rather lose the money than be treated like an afterthought.
R2: Nikhil, 35, a freelance translator, finished a rush job for a client who then announced he would pay only a small fraction of the agreed fee, around fifteen percent, citing 'budget changes'. Nikhil signed the revised invoice without protest. In every dealing, however lopsided the terms, he goes along as long as he ends up with something.
R3: At a flea market, Colm, 67, was offered ten dollars for a clock the dealer clearly knew was worth a hundred. Insulted by the lowball, Colm packed the clock away and later gave it to a charity shop, pocketing nothing. He would sooner walk away empty-handed than let anyone profit from treating him that way.
R4: When the fence between their yards collapsed, Doreen, 70, paid the full one-hundred-fifty-dollar repair. Her neighbor offered to contribute twenty dollars, take it or leave it. Doreen took it. Whatever the split, she reasons, twenty dollars in hand beats nothing at all, and she accepts any terms that leave her even slightly ahead.

After seeing the proposed price set by the data provider, the broker will decide whether to accept

- The data provider receives a bonus equal to the final price set.
- The broker receives $12 from the research team, pays the provider the set price, and keeps the

- If the broker rejects, the sale does not take place and both participants receive $0.

The computer selected a starting price of $12.

You may change the price by any amount between -$12 and $0. A negative change means that you
